thread.title: Can a Big Buyback Save Apple Stock?

author: Ashraf Eassa, The Motley Fool
title: Can a Big Buyback Save Apple Stock?
text:
Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL) stock has lost a substantial amount of its value over the last couple of months as reports swirled that iPhone sales weren't quite as robust as Apple had hoped. (Those fears were confirmed when the company reduced its financial guidance for the first quarter of its fiscal 2019.)
One key part of Apple's capital return strategy is to use its free cash flow -- as well as the significant amount of excess cash that's sitting on its balance sheet -- to repurchase stock.
Apple's iPhone X. More Image source: Apple.
In fact, at the end of the fourth quarter of Apple's fiscal 2018, the company had $71 billion left of the $100 billion share repurchase authorization that its board of directors approved back on May 1, 2018. Apple has likely utilized a material portion of that authorization over the last several months.
So, you might be asking yourself this: Can Apple use its share repurchase program to help boost its stock?
The answer to that is complicated. Let's take a closer look.
How buybacks can help A key benefit of share buyback programs is that they can increase a company's earnings per share (EPS) by reducing the number of shares outstanding. The math here is simple -- divide a company's earnings by a lower share count, and EPS gets bigger for a fixed amount of earnings.
Share buybacks thus amplify a company's EPS growth over time. Remember that Apple rakes in a lot of cash, and it's not shy about deploying that cash to gobble up its own shares. (In fact, Apple executives have been pretty explicit about preferring buybacks to dividends because of their -- seemingly eternal -- opinion that Apple shares are undervalued.)
The chart below shows the effect that Apple's buyback program has had on its share count over the years:
AAPL Average Diluted Shares Outstanding (Quarterly) Chart More Apple Average Diluted Shares Outstanding (Quarterly) , data by YCharts
Apple wouldn't be able to report the EPS figures that it can today if the company hadn't bought back all of that stock. And since stocks are often valued based on metrics like price-to-earnings, the lower share count certainly helps improve those metrics and, potentially, the attractiveness of Apple stock.
Here comes the "but" Apple is a technology stock, and technology companies that aren't growing or that are expected to deliver slow growth for a while don't tend to command a lot of respect in the market. (A company's price-to-earnings ratio can be a reasonable proxy for that "respect" -- a higher P/E ratio can be a sign that investors collectively see a brighter future for a company than they do for a company with a lower ratio.)
